questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3{t}^{2}-8t+4,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds.  The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when $t=2\,\text{s},$ determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-8t+4)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-4{t}^{2}+4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(2)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(2)^{3}-4(2)^{2}+4(2)+C \\ 0 & =8-16+8+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-4{t}^{2}+4t.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{3}-4{t}^{2}+4t=t(t-2)^{2}>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/9254ea32fc55b2a703e52f55f4292d9708eef63ae147a9f1d2eac40b85eff319.png)

From the graph, we see that $v>0$ whenever $0<t<2$ or $t>2.$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=1-2t$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=-6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s}$, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =(4)-(4)^{2}+C \\ -6 & =4-16+C \\ -6 & =-12+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+t+6.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
-{t}^{2}+t+6=-({t}^{2}-t-6)=-(t+2)(t-3)>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/74db16dc00f5d08637cef02960409b7fd15c4bd3c19f577fa5a1f30ac8c402d3.png)

From the graph, we see that $v>0$ whenever $0<t<3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=15-3t,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=14\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
questions.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 15-3t & =0 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(15-3t) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(5)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (15-3t)\text{d}t \\  & =15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=14.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15(1)-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+C & =14 \\ C & =\frac{3}{2}-1\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}+15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(5)=\frac{1}{2}+15(5)-\frac{3}{2}(5)^{2}=38\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+4.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$

If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

The maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=$

questions.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$  

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & =0 \\ 5t & =\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{5}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer.  

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{5},\frac{2\pi }{5},\frac{3\pi }{5},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\  & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{5},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{5}) & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-50<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{5})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{5}.$ Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+C & =2 \\ -2+C & =2 \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
v(t)=4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{max}} & =v(\frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =6\,\text{m}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the maximum velocity  ${v}_{\text{max}}=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at  $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=16t-{t}^{3},$ where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=44\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
questions.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 16t-{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(16-{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ t(4-t)(4+t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(16t-{t}^{3}) \\  & =16-3{t}^{2} \\ {v}^{″}(4) & =16-3(4)^{2} \\  & =-32\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(4)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (16t-{t}^{3})\text{d}t \\  & =8{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(2)=44.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}8(2)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(2)^{4}+C & =44 \\ 32-4+C & =44\,⟹\,C=16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=16+8{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(4)=16+8(4)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{4}=80\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\sqrt{t}-t,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\sqrt{t}-t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{6} & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{6}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}=0 \\ 4{t}^{3/2}-3{t}^{2}=0 \\ {t}^{3/2}(4-3{t}^{1/2}) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{16}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{16}{9}\,\text{s}.$

\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{3} & =\frac{8}{3}(1)^{3/2}+C \\ \frac{7}{3} & =\frac{8}{3}+C \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{8}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{3}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{8}{3}{t}^{3/2} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ 8{t}^{3/2} & =1 \\ {t}^{3/2} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ t & ={(\frac{1}{8})}^{2/3}=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{s}.$

If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=9\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(9)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\sqrt{9}+C \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\sqrt{t}-2.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{t}-2 & =0 \\ \sqrt{t} & =2 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3{t}^{2}-6t-4,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=30\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=5\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-6t-4)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(5)=30.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}30 & =(5)^{3}-3(5)^{2}-4(5)+C \\ 30 & =125-75-20+C \\ 30 & =30+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t & =0 \\ t({t}^{2}-3t-4) & =0 \\ t(t-4)(t+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $t=-1,0,4.$

Since $t>0,$ we discard solutions $t=-1,0.$ 
Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 3t^2+2t-6,$ where $t > 0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+2t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-6t+C\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the particle is stationary at the time $t=0.$ This means $v(0) = 0,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}-6(0)+C \\ 0 & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore the velocity of the particle is

$$
v(t) = t^3+t^2-6t.
$$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v > 0.$ This gives

$$
t^3+t^2-6t = t(t+3)(t-2) > 0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/03b5ff6282d59038cbb355c0c3f017b544f286228ba4c3a82329897b4b43674c.png)

The particle moves to the right when $v(t)$ is positive. So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when $t>2.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 6t-3t^2,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s,$ calculate the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t) = 0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t) = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3t(2-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t> 0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t = 2\,\textrm s.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =6-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =6-6(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v''(2) <      0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\textrm s.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+C & =2 \\ 3-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) =3t^2-t^3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s
$$

So the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ is reached at $t=2\,\textrm s.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) =2t-6$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s$, determine the moments in time when the particle is stationary.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-6)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-6t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) =4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 4 & =-5+C \\ C & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^2-6t + 9.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+9 & =0 \\ (t-3)^{2} & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=3 \,\textrm s.$
